newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy pledges crackdown on 'dolce vita' turncoats.
newsitem.headline: Italy pledges crackdown on 'dolce vita' turncoats.

text.p: Italian leaders promised on Tuesday to review the treatment of Mafia turncoats after a murdered policeman's widow said they should be punished not paid.

Concetta Montinaro made her attack on the financial and other benefits enjoyed by gangsters who turn state's evidence at the trial of some 40 Mafiosi accused of the bombing murder in 1992 of investigator Giovanni Falcone and three police guards.
"I feel humiliated and insulted by the attitude that rewards and praises turncoats instead of punishing them," said Montinaro, whose husband Antonio was among the dead.
Several of the defendants at the trial over the Falcone murder, the Mob's most shocking attack, have turned state's evidence but Montinaro said she could never forgive them.
"I don't accept that a turncoat should be paid maintenance, continue to live like a lord and enjoy his children," Montinaro, left to bring up a young son alone, told the court in Sicily.
Her criticism at the weekend re-ignited a debate in Italy over the privileges reserved for turncoats, known as 'pentiti', and the reliability of their information.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who called Montinaro's words 'touching', said turncoats were an important weapon in the war on organised crime but acknowledged that tighter rules were needed on their entitlement to privileges.
"There are balances that have to be respected and in many cases they have not been respected," Prodi told reporters.
Official figures show 1,244 former criminals plus relatives are covered by Italy's witness protection scheme, which costs the state some 100 billion lire ($650 million) a year.
Ottaviano Del Turco, chairman of parliament's anti-Mafia commission, said the body would meet on Thursday to discuss changes in the way turncoats are treated.
The witness protection scheme was established after the killing of Falcone.

It has proved highly valuable, with "boss of bosses" Salvatore 'The Beast' Riina and a string of top mobsters all arrested as a result of unprecedented information from gangsters who broke the Mafia's deadly code of "omerta" or silence.

The system is also controversial. Many defendants on trial as a result of turncoat evidence, including former prime minister Giulio Andreotti, argue that their accusers are lying to protect their own skins and stay out of jail.

Andreotti, charged with Mafia ties and complicity in murder, expressed outrage last month after one of the chief prosecution witnesses, ex-Mafioso Balduccio di Maggio, testified that he had received 500 million lire ($325,000) from the state.

Another of Andreotti's accusers, and one of Falcone's alleged killers, former boss Salvatore Cancemi, testified on Tuesday that he received 2.8 million lire ($1,800) a month. "It's enough to stop me from starving," Cancemi told a court.
Hard right politician Gianfranco Fini called the payments scandalous and expressed full support for Montinaro's outburst.
"It's shameful that a policeman earns 1.5 million lire or so a month and that a pentito get two million plus board and lodging from the state," Fini told Italian television.
